differences.title: 1. PRIMARY USE
differences.leftDesc: OAuth 2.0 orchestrates delegated access so an app obtains tokens to call APIs. It doesn’t inherently define user login UI; it specifies flows for authorization, token issuance, and scope-based access control.
differences.rightDesc: SAML 2.0 is designed primarily for enterprise SSO. An IdP issues signed authentication assertions consumed by service providers, establishing a user session based on identity statements rather than API-scoped token authorization.

differences.title: 2. TOKEN/ARTIFACT SHAPE
differences.leftDesc: OAuth typically issues opaque or JWT-like access tokens alongside optional refresh tokens. The token is presented to resource servers, which validate signature/introspection and enforce scope/claims for each request.
differences.rightDesc: SAML uses XML-based assertions delivered via browser redirects or form posts. Service providers verify XML signatures, validate conditions (audience, time window), and map attributes to an account to create a local session.

differences.title: 3. TRANSPORT & BROWSER FLOW
differences.leftDesc: OAuth authorization code flow redirects the browser to the authorization server, then returns to a client callback with an authorization code. The client exchanges it server-to-server for tokens, often using PKCE to mitigate interception.
differences.rightDesc: SAML commonly relies on HTTP-Redirect or HTTP-POST bindings from the IdP to the SP. The browser carries the assertion artifact, and the SP validates it to log the user in, with less emphasis on token exchange backchannels.

differences.title: 4. CLAIMS & POLICIES
differences.leftDesc: OAuth access decisions are typically driven by scopes (and sometimes audience/issuer) embedded in tokens. Resource servers interpret claims to authorize specific API operations without necessarily sharing a global identity session.
differences.rightDesc: SAML assertions carry authentication statements and attribute statements. The SP enforces assertion conditions and uses attributes for account linking and authorization, often relying on enterprise-defined attribute contracts and role mappings.

differences.title: 5. CRYPTO & SIGNING PRACTICES
differences.leftDesc: OAuth implementations may use JWTs with JWS (signatures) and optionally JWE (encryption). Some deployments keep access tokens opaque and use introspection endpoints for server-side verification and revocation semantics.
differences.rightDesc: SAML assertions are typically protected using XML Signature for integrity and, optionally, XML Encryption. Signature verification includes canonicalization and reference validation, and misconfiguration can lead to subtle trust-validation bugs.

differences.title: 6. SESSION LIFECYCLE
differences.leftDesc: OAuth tokens allow stateless API authorization: a resource server can validate claims per request. Revocation/expiry are handled via short TTLs, refresh token rotation, and optional revocation endpoints or introspection.
differences.rightDesc: SAML is centered on federated sessions between IdP and SP. Logouts and session termination often require SAML Single Logout or coordinated session handling, with longer-lived browser sessions common in enterprise deployments.

differences.title: 7. MODERN ECOSYSTEM & ADOPTION
differences.leftDesc: OAuth 2.0 underpins modern authorization patterns for APIs, mobile, and SPAs, and is frequently paired with OpenID Connect for identity. It fits naturally with REST/JSON services and cloud-native token validation.
differences.rightDesc: SAML 2.0 remains prevalent in enterprise identity platforms and SaaS ecosystems needing mature, configurable SSO. Its XML-based contracts integrate well with legacy tooling, though operational complexity can be higher.
